newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi Kurds vow to keep PKK out of northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi Kurds vow to keep PKK out of northern Iraq.

text.p: Turkey's Iraqi Kurdish allies have vowed to keep the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas out of northern Iraq once Ankara's week-old campaign against the rebels is over.

"We will not allow the PKK back into any region controlled by KDP...The PKK will no longer be able to operate in any manner whatsoever in any region controlled by the PKK," senior Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) member Sami Abderrahman told Reuters in an interview.
"The PKK has made our lives hell here. There are 350 villages along the Turkish-Iraqi border to which displaced persons are unable to return because of the PKK," he said.

More than 10,000 Turkish troops poured into northern Iraq last week to begin a major cross-border operation in pursuit of PKK separatists who use northern Iraq as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
The operation has been criticised by Turkey's Western allies and the United Nations, and unnerved its neighbours.

According to Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency, Syria, Iraq and Iran have massed forces near the borders of the Kurdish "safe haven". The report was partially confirmed by the pro-PKK MED TV, which is based in Belgium, and the anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress (INC). Damascus, Baghdad and Tehran have not commented on the reports.
Abderrahman did not say how long he expected the incursion to last, but said Turkey would have to pull out eventually.
"We will not accept a permanent Turkish military presence in northern Iraq, neither will Baghdad nor the Arab world," he said in the interview, which took place on Tuesday.
Baghdad, which has criticised the incursion throughout as a violation of international law, lashed out again on Wednesday, warning it had the right to answer accordingly.

"Turkey must stop acting like a phoney policeman and realise that the era of ageing and sick empires is gone forever," Issam Khalil, Iraq's ambassador to Greece, said in Athens, warning that Baghdad was entitled to "reply accordingly to Turkey's aggressive act."
Turkey says it moved in at the request of the KDP, which controls the Turkish border regions of the Kurdish-run area.

But Abderrahman denied that Turkey and the KDP had made a pact against the rebels: "It is the PKK that has brought the Turkish army into northern Iraq," he said. "There has been no deal (between Turkey and the KDP)."
Abderrahman said the PKK sought control on both sides of the Turkish-northern Iraqi border in order to control drugs trading:
"The PKK's main activity involves smuggling drugs around the world," he said. "It is an international drugs cartel."
Turkish politicians have often said the PKK trades drugs to finance its guerrilla activities.

The INC reported heavy fighting between Turkish troops and the PKK around Chamcha, to the north of Dohuk -- the main town in the area -- and between the KDP and the PKK in the Mateen mountains, 60 kilometres (40 miles) to the northeast of Dohuk.
An INC spokesman said Turkish artillery bombarded PKK positions on the nearby Gara mountains from morning to nightfall on Wednesday, inflicting heavy casualties. He gave no figures.
There were reports of busy troop movement over the past two days both in northern Iraq and across the border.

Witnesses said Turkish troops had set up tents and a communication space on a hilltop overlooking the border town of Zakho, which itself remained quiet with a relatively small Turkish military presence.
The Turkish army said on Wednesday it had killed 1,146 PKK rebels during the incursion and captured the Zap valley which it says was the main base for the PKK in the area.
A further 152 PKK guerillas were either captured or missing, the army statement said.
PKK sources say the number is exaggerated and KDP sources indicated that the PKK may have left the region ahead of the arrival of the Turks, forewarned by a long buildup.
The incursion has been carried out under a strict news blackout, making the size and scope of the operation impossible to confirm.
